extracted.intended_audience: parties and practitioners (petitioner/patent owner counsel) involved in AIA trials before the PTAB
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and litigating petitions, motions, discovery, testimony, and related filings in AIA trial proceedings (Inter Partes Review, Post-Grant Review, and Derivation) before the Patent Trial and Appeal Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to seal — provisional sealing on receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: A document or thing to be sealed may file a motion to seal concurrent with the filing of the document or thing. The document or thing will be provisionally sealed on receipt of the motion and remain so pending the outcome of the decision on motion. 37 C.F.R. § 42.14.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File the motion to seal at the same time as filing the confidential material to obtain provisional sealing pending the Board's decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective orders — must be proposed and approved
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may file a motion to seal where the motion contains a proposed protective order. A protective order is not entered by default but must be proposed by one or more parties and must be approved and entered by the Board. Protective orders may be issued for good cause by the Board to protect a party from disclosing confidential information. 37 C.F.R. § 42.54.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines on proposing a protective order, including a Default Protective Order, are provided in Appendix B. A document will be protected on receipt of the motion and remain so pending the Board's decision. If the motion is not granted, the submitting party may seek expungement; otherwise, the information may be publicly disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential information submitted with a petition — sealing and access rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner filing confidential information with a petition may, concurrent with the filing, file a motion to seal with a proposed protective order and is not required to serve the confidential information. 37 C.F.R. § 42.55.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner may seek entry of the default protective order or an alternative. Patent owner access prior to institution is governed by agreement to the default order, agreement to petitioner's requested order, joint protective order, or Board entry of an order. The Office anticipates use of the electronic filing system to register such agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expungement of confidential information
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidential information subject to a protective order ordinarily becomes public 45 days after denial of a petition to institute a trial or 45 days after final judgment in a trial. A party may file a motion to expunge information from the record prior to it becoming public. 37 C.F.R. § 42.56.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule balances party confidentiality needs with the public interest in file history. Parties are encouraged to redact sensitive information where possible rather than seek to seal entire documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation — sealing conception dates
rubrics_metrics.description: A party in a derivation submitting dates of conception to establish inventorship may file those dates under seal and request that an opponent not be given access to the conception dates until the opponent’s conception dates have been provided to the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sealing conception dates can be used to protect sensitive inventorship evidence until reciprocal disclosures are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequenced discovery — discovery periods and focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules and Scheduling Order provide a sequenced discovery process upon institution of the trial; each party is provided respective discovery periods, beginning with the patent owner. Discovery before the Board is focused on what the parties reasonably need to respond to the grounds raised by an opponent so the scope of the trial continually narrows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequencing allows meaningful discovery before motions/oppositions and promotes efficiency; Scheduling Order will set timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine discovery — what it includes and authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine discovery includes: (1) production of any exhibit cited in a paper or testimony; (2) the cross-examination of the other side's declarants; and (3) relevant information that is inconsistent with a position advanced during the proceeding. Board authorization is not required for routine discovery, although the Board will set times for conducting it in its Scheduling Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine discovery is intended to place parties on a level playing field and streamline proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of inconsistent statements and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party relies on expert affidavits or surprising/unexpected results, the party must provide non-privileged work or evidence inconsistent with those contentions (e.g., non-privileged work undertaken by petitioner, or patent owner’s non-privileged evidence inconsistent with unexpected properties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: petitioner relying on expert claiming method cannot be carried out must produce inconsistent non-privileged work; patent owner relying on unexpected results should provide inconsistent evidence to petitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness expenses — presenting party bears costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden and expense of producing a witness for redirect or cross examination should normally fall on the party presenting the witness, including expert witness fees or travel expenses; same rules apply if testimony is presented by transcript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties presenting testimony by affidavit should arrange to make the witness available for cross-examination and bear associated expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document translation — English requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: All proceedings before the Board will be conducted in English. Translations must be provided for documents produced in discovery and all documents relied on or used during proceedings; otherwise, documents not accompanied by English translations will not be considered by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide timely English translations for any non-English materials to ensure the Board will consider them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional discovery — motion required and standards vary
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for additional discovery must be in the form of a motion, although parties may agree to such discovery among themselves. Parties to an AIA trial can generally seek the same types of discovery available under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure. The standard for granting requests varies with the proceeding: an 'interests of justice' standard applies in IPR and derivation proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 42.51(b)(2)), whereas a more liberal 'good cause' standard applies in PGR proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 42.224).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In IPRs, Board guidance primarily follows the Garmin precedential decision; parties in PGRs should also consult Bloomberg decision for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garmin factor 1 — more than possibility/mere allegation
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere possibility of finding something useful, and mere allegation that something useful will be found, are insufficient. The party requesting discovery should already be in possession of evidence or reasoning 'tending to show beyond speculation' that something useful will be uncovered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moving party should identify threshold evidence or reasoning demonstrating likely usefulness of requested discovery (examples: identifying specific pieces of evidence or showing why depositions will be informative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Garmin factor 2 — litigation positions and underlying basis generally not discoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking for the other party’s litigation positions and the underlying basis for those positions is not necessary in the interest of justice; there is a proper time and place for presentation of arguments and evidence, and a party may not use discovery to alter Board trial procedures (contention interrogatories typically not permitted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests for expert reports and deposition transcripts from parallel litigation are often denied when sought to probe IPR positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garmin factor 3 — ability to generate equivalent information by other means
rubrics_metrics.description: Information that a party can reasonably figure out or assemble without a discovery request would not be in the interest of justice. The Board wants to know the ability of the requesting party to generate the requested information without discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the requesting party can obtain the information by other reasonable means, additional discovery is less likely to be granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garmin factor 4 — requests must be easily understandable
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery requests should be easily understandable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft requests clearly and precisely to facilitate Board review and limit disputes over scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Garmin factor 5 — requests must not be overly burdensome
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests must not be overly burdensome to answer given the expedited nature of Inter Partes Review. Burden includes financial burden, human resources, and burden on IPR schedule. Requests should be sensible and reasonably tailored according to a genuine need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to address Garmin factors and to justify focused, narrowly tailored requests; Board may discuss during conference call.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional discovery commonly sought issues — focused, narrow requests favored
rubrics_metrics.description: Two frequently sought areas are identifying real parties-in-interest and secondary evidence of non-obviousness. Narrowly focused requests on these issues may be permitted; overbroad or unfocused requests are likely to be denied as overly burdensome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: focused discovery relating to communications about IPR preparation may be granted; broad discovery about copying or post-oral-argument RPI matters may be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compelled testimony — authorization and formats
rubrics_metrics.description: A party can request authorization to compel testimony under 35 U.S.C. § 24. If granted, testimony may be (1) ex parte, subject to subsequent cross-examination, or (2) inter partes. Parties should discuss which procedure is appropriate prior to moving. See Appendix D for guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider procedural approach and consult Appendix D; coordinate with opposing party before moving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory initial disclosures — statutory and regulatory compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 42.51(a) provides for mandatory initial disclosures either by agreement (subparagraph (a)(1)) or, where parties fail to agree, by motion, if granted (subparagraph (a)(2)). To proceed under (a)(1), the parties must submit any agreement on initial disclosures no later than filing the patent owner’s preliminary response or by expiration of time for filing such a response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties agree, disclosures must be timely filed; upon institution, the parties may automatically take discovery of the information identified in initial disclosures and such disclosures should be filed as exhibits as soon as reasonably practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial disclosures — Option 1 (Rule 26(a)(1)(A)-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Option 1 (modeled after Rule 26(a)(1)(A)) requires disclosure of: (1) name and, if known, address and telephone of each individual likely to have discoverable information and the subjects of that information (unless solely for impeachment); and (2) a copy or description by category and location of all documents, ESI, and tangible things in the disclosing party's possession, custody, or control that may be used to support claims or defenses (unless solely for impeachment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These disclosures enable immediate discovery upon institution; file disclosures as exhibits to permit related discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial disclosures — Option 2 (extensive disclosures for certain petitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Option 2 (more extensive) requires, if petition seeks cancellation based on alleged prior non-published public disclosure, statement identifying persons likely to know of the disclosure, documents relating to the disclosure, and details (complete description, photographs, chemical analysis, computer code) and locations and whether the petitioner will produce such items. If petition seeks cancellation based on alleged obviousness, petitioner must similarly identify persons and documents relating to secondary indicia of non-obviousness and specifics about items and production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Option 2's two-part list (I and II) contains five sub-items each specifying the depth of contact and evidence disclosures expected; these disclosures also become available for discovery upon institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live testimony — limited circumstances and factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-examination may be ordered to take place in presence of an administrative patent judge; the Board will permit live testimony where demeanor is critical (e.g., derivation issues, alleged misconduct, inventors providing declaration testimony to antedate references). Live testimony is necessary only in limited circumstances and is approached case-by-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors from K-40 Electronics include importance of witness testimony (potentially case-dispositive) and whether witness is a fact witness; expert credibility often turns on theory plausibility, not demeanor. Prior provision of declarations affects admissibility (see DePuy). See Appendix D and Section II.M for additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Times and locations for witness cross-examination — default time limits and reasonable location
rubrics_metrics.description: Default time limits (37 C.F.R. § 42.53): compelled direct examination 7 hours, cross-examination 4 hours, redirect 2 hours. For uncompelled direct testimony, default cross 7 hours, redirect 4 hours, recross 2 hours. Testimony may be taken at any reasonable U.S. location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should attempt to agree on location; Board will handle disputes, typically via conference call. See Appendix D for more information.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-discovery — default Model Order and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of e-discovery costs, the Office adopts a default Model Order Regarding E-Discovery (Appendix C). Except for routine discovery, the default Model Order will be entered in a proceeding whenever discovery of ESI is sought. Parties desiring production of ESI as part of additional discovery should raise the matter with the Board in a timely fashion before discovery is scheduled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect the Model Order to govern ESI discovery; timely raise ESI issues to the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony — admissibility, qualification, and content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony may be submitted with the petition, preliminary response, and at other stages as ordered. Expert testimony is generally permitted where the expert’s specialized knowledge will help the trier of fact. Experts must be qualified by knowledge, skill, experience, training, or education (Fed. R. Evid. 702). Expert testimony is presented as an affidavit or declaration. The testimony must be based on sufficient facts and data (Fed. R. Evid. 702(b)), be the product of reliable principles and methods (702(c)), and reliably apply those principles to the facts (702(d)). 37 C.F.R. § 42.65(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of an advanced degree does not preclude qualification if experience suffices. Expert testimony that does not disclose underlying facts or data may be entitled to little or no weight. Experts may explain technology, level of skill, prior art teachings, reasons to combine references, reasonable expectation of success, and weigh objective indicia of nonobviousness. Expert testimony cannot substitute for disclosure in a prior art reference or supply missing claim elements; it can explain patents/printed publications but not provide the missing disclosure itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference and word limits — risk of non-consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 42.24(a) sets word limits and § 42.6(a)(3) prohibits incorporating arguments by reference from one document into another. Parties that incorporate expert testimony by reference in petitions, motions, or replies without explanation risk having the testimony not considered by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with word limits; avoid improper incorporation by reference. See Cisco Systems v. C-Cation for example where incorporation risked non-consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word count and page limits — specific limits and certification
rubrics_metrics.description: Word and page limits apply: 14,000 words for IPR and derivation petitions, 18,700 words for PGR petitions (37 C.F.R. § 42.24(a)). Motions (other than motions to amend) are limited to 15 pages; motions to amend limited to 25 pages. Patent owner preliminary responses and responses to petitions are subject to same word limits as the petition. Replies and oppositions have specific limits: replies to patent owner responses to petitions limited to 5,600 words; replies to oppositions to motions to amend limited to 12 pages; replies to all other oppositions limited to 5 pages. Sur-replies, if authorized, are subject to same limits. 37 C.F.R. § 42.24(d) requires that any paper with type-volume limits include a certification stating the number of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exemptions to word count include table of contents, table of authorities, mandatory notices, certificate of service, or appendix of exhibits or claim listing (but not grounds for standing). Parties may rely on their word-processing software for certification. Abusive tactics to circumvent word counts can lead to briefs not being considered; Board generally accepts certifications unless obvious abuse—raise violations promptly and attempt to remedy before approaching the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony and expert opinions must disclose underlying facts or data
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits expressing an opinion of an expert must disclose the underlying facts or data upon which the opinion is based. See Fed. R. Evid. 705; 37 C.F.R. § 42.65.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinions without disclosure of underlying facts or data may be given little or no weight; unsupported assertions are not credited (see Rohm & Haas Co. v. Brotech Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests and data — provide explanatory information
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties relying on scientific tests and data (e.g., infrared spectroscopy, HPLC) should provide any other information they believe would assist the Board in understanding the significance of the test or data, in addition to the explanation required by 37 C.F.R. § 42.65.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide relevant protocols, raw data, explanations, and anything needed to interpret scientific evidence so Board can assess significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia of nonobviousness — Board will review when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining obviousness, the Board will review any objective evidence of nonobviousness proffered by the patent owner where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enter objective indicia into the record with adequate explanation and supporting evidence; expert testimony can explain how to weigh such evidence against unpatentability evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition minimum procedural compliance and filing requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a filing date, the petition must meet certain minimum standards (see 37 C.F.R. § 42.106 and 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)). For IPR a complete petition must be filed with the required fee, certificate of service for petition/fee/evidence, a certification that the patent is eligible for IPR and the petitioner is not barred or estopped, and identification of claims being challenged and specific basis for challenge (37 C.F.R. § 42.104). Similar petition requirements apply to PGR and derivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all statutory and regulatory filing requirements are met to obtain a proper filing date and avoid procedural defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for institution thresholds — preponderance of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof before the Board is a preponderance of the evidence standard. 37 C.F.R. § 42.1(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame petition and evidence to satisfy preponderance standard for institution and for merits determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions practice — general requirement of prior authorization and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings begin with a petition; additional relief must be requested by motion (37 C.F.R. § 42.20(a)). Generally, a motion will not be entered without prior Board authorization (37 C.F.R. § 42.20(b)). Exceptions include motions where impractical to seek prior authorization (motions to seal and motions filed with a petition, e.g., to waive word count/page limits) and motions where authorization is automatically granted (requests for rehearing and motions to exclude evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorization is typically obtained during an initial conference call within one month of institution. Parties should request a conference call for immediate relief or later-arising issues; conference calls let the Board decide many procedural issues promptly and simplify proceedings.
